1687.content:
Container CPU is converted to whole OCPUs (1 OCPU is 2 vCPUs, at least 1), and memory is rounded
up to whole GB within 1 to 64 GB per OCPU.

1688.content:
Services receive their dependencies as `<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_BUCKET` and
`<ID>_ENDPOINT`. Container instances cannot inject secrets, so a dependency's credentials arrive
as `<ID>_CREDENTIALS_REF`, the Vault secret OCID. The application reads it with its own identity,
for example a resource principal with `read secret-bundles`. Resources on other providers can read
the same secret through `readSecret` (fields `username`, `password`, `host`, `port`, `database`,
`url`).

1689.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning      |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------ |
| `tenancyOcid`  | yes      | Tenancy OCID |

1690.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning              |
| -------------- | -------- | -------------------- |
| `userOcid`     | yes      | OCID of the API user |

1691.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                            |
| -------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `fingerprint`  | yes      | Fingerprint of the API signing key |

1692.content:
| `config` field    | Required | Meaning                                                                             |
| ----------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compartmentOcid` | yes      | Compartment where resources are created (the tenancy OCID for the root compartment) |

1693.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                    |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `namespace`    | yes      | Object Storage namespace (`oci os ns get`) |

1694.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                            |
| -------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `stateBucket`  | yes      | Existing bucket for OpenTofu state |

1695.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                  |
| -------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `vaultOcid`    | no       | Vault for generated database credentials |

1696.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                 |
| -------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `keyOcid`      | no       | AES master encryption key in that vault |

1697.content:
Set `vaultOcid` and `keyOcid` together. Without them, every PostgreSQL database creates its own
vault and software key, and validation shows a warning, because OCI keeps a deleted vault in a
pending deletion state for at least 7 days.

1698.content:
| Field        | What it is                                                                                                 |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `privateKey` | PEM private key of the API signing key (PKCS#1 or PKCS#8, no passphrase), with line breaks written as `\n` |

1699.content:
| Field              | What it is                                             |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `stateAccessKeyId` | Customer secret key id, used only for the state bucket |

1700.content:
| Field                  | What it is                                                |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `stateSecretAccessKey` | Customer secret key value, used only for the state bucket |

1701.content:
The private key reaches OpenTofu only as `TF_VAR_oci_private_key` in the runner environment, read
by a sensitive root variable. The state keys reach it only as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` for the S3 backend. None of them is written to the configuration.

1702.content:
Create a user (or use an existing one) in a group that has the permissions listed below, then give
it an API signing key:

1703.content: The upload prints the key fingerprint. The private key must not have a passphrase.

1704.content:
OrkStage never creates the state bucket. Buckets reached through the S3 compatibility API must be
in the compartment designated for it (the root compartment unless you changed it with
`oci os ns update-metadata`).

1705.content:
The customer secret key output has an `id` (the access key id) and a `key` (the secret access
key, shown only once).

1706.content: Put the vault and key OCIDs in `vaultOcid` and `keyOcid`.

1707.content:
Validation checks the configuration format, signs a request that reads the compartment (the
compartment name becomes the target identity) and checks that the state bucket answers.

1708.content: Policies for the group of the API user, with `<c>` the target compartment:

1709.content:
The state bucket also needs `manage objects` for the group in the S3 designated compartment. The
last statement is needed only for bucket expiry rules (`retentionDays`). With a shared vault,
`use vaults` and `use keys` on that vault are enough instead of `manage`.

1710.content:
Regions are OCI region identifiers such as `us-ashburn-1` or `sa-saopaulo-1`. Only the commercial
realm (`oc1`, `oraclecloud.com`) is supported. Subnets are regional and span every availability
domain, so `availabilityZones` does not change the layout. Regions with a single availability
domain spread workloads across fault domains instead.

1711.content:
| Capability            | Action    | Parameters | Effect                                           |
| --------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `container-instances` | `restart` | none       | Restarts every container instance of the service |

1712.content: Container instances have no autoscaling. `replicas` is a fixed instance count.

1713.content:
A new image or setting replaces the container instances. New instances start before the old
ones stop, and the plan treats this as a routine rollout.

1714.content:
Private registry credentials are not configured. Use public images or a registry the instances
can reach without credentials.

1715.content:
PostgreSQL storage grows automatically, so `storageGiB` only feeds estimates. `publicAccess` is
not supported: endpoints are private to the VCN. High availability adds a second node on
regionally durable storage. The generated password is kept in OpenTofu state and in the Vault
secret, never in outputs.

1716.content:
OCI Cache has no password. Access is limited to the VCN, clients must use TLS, and there are at
most four replicas.

1717.content: Buckets must be empty before they are deleted.

1718.content:
The load balancer listens on HTTP port 80. TLS certificates are not managed yet. In production,
delete protection is on.

1719.content: State locking uses no lock file. OrkStage runs one operation per resource at a time.

1721.content: Deploy static sites, image based services, Postgres and Key Value on Render through its REST API. API key, workspace id, plans, triggers and limits.

1731.content:
The Render adapter is covered by unit tests. It has not been verified against a live workspace
yet.

1732.content:
The Render adapter drives the Render REST API (`https://api.render.com/v1`) directly: no
OpenTofu, no modules and no state store. Resources are found by name in the target workspace, so
repeating a deployment converges the existing resource instead of creating a second one.

1733.content:
| Template resource | Capability                     | Render resource | Notes                                                              |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `web.frontend`    | `render-static-site` (default) | Static site     | Built from a Git repository, custom domains, pull request previews |

1734.content:
| Template resource           | Capability                     | Render resource            | Notes                                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compute.container-service` | `render-web-service` (default) | Web service, image runtime | Used when `public: true`. Plan from `cpu` and `memoryMiB`. |

1735.content:
| Template resource           | Capability               | Render resource                | Notes                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compute.container-service` | `render-private-service` | Private service, image runtime | Used when `public` is false. Reachable only inside the workspace and region. |

1736.content:
| Template resource     | Capability                  | Render resource | Notes                                                     |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database.postgresql` | `render-postgres` (default) | Render Postgres | Plan by size. High availability on plans with a full CPU. |

1737.content:
| Template resource | Capability                   | Render resource                     | Notes                      |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `cache.redis`     | `render-key-value` (default) | Render Key Value, Valkey compatible | Plan by size. Single node. |

1743.content:
| Size     | Postgres | Key Value   |
| -------- | -------- | ----------- |
| `xlarge` | `4c-16g` | not offered |

1744.content:
Services get the smallest plan that has at least the requested vCPU and memory (`0.5c-512mb`,
`1c-2g`, `2c-4g` and so on). Prices in the catalog are approximate list prices, not an invoice.

1745.content:
Services and static sites receive their dependencies as environment variables with the shared
names such as `<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT` and `<ID>_URL`. Credentials come from the dependency's
`secret_ref`:

1746.content:
A Render Postgres or Key Value in the same workspace and region is wired with its internal
connection string and internal host name. This applies to services only: static sites are built
outside the private network.

1747.content:
Credentials from any other provider are read through OrkStage at deploy time and stored as
Render environment variables, which Render keeps encrypted.

1748.content:
Values never appear in outputs, logs or error messages. The adapter owns the environment of the
services it manages: variables added by hand in the dashboard are replaced on the next apply.
Changes to settings or variables start one deploy so they take effect.

1749.content:
Postgres and Key Value publish `secret_ref` as `render-postgres://<id>` and `render-kv://<id>`.
`readSecret` returns `url` (external connection string), `internalUrl`, `username`, `password`,
`host`, `port` and, for Postgres, `database`, so a frontend on another provider can connect.

1750.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ownerId`      | yes      | Workspace id, `tea-<id>` for a team workspace or `usr-<id>` for a personal one. Find it in the workspace settings or with `GET /v1/owners`. |

1751.content:
| `config` field         | Required | Meaning                                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `registryCredentialId` | no       | Registry credential (`rgc-<id>`) Render uses to pull private images. Create it under Workspace settings, Registry credentials. |

1752.content:
Create an API key in the Render dashboard under Account settings, API keys. A key acts as its user
on every workspace that user belongs to, so use a dedicated user where you can.

1753.content: The secret behind `credentialRef` is the bare key or a JSON object:

1754.content:
Validation checks the configuration offline, then reads `GET /v1/owners/{ownerId}`. The workspace
name becomes the target identity. A rejected key, or a workspace the key's user cannot see, fails
validation with a message that never contains the key.

1755.content:
Render builds static sites from a repository it can read. Before the first deploy, connect the Git
provider (GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket) to the workspace in the Render dashboard and grant the
Render app access to the repository named in `source.repository`. Without that access the create
call fails with a validation error from Render.

1756.content:
Custom domains in `domains` are added to the site. Point their DNS at Render to verify them. The
`url` output switches to the first verified custom domain; otherwise it is the `onrender.com` URL.

1757.content:
Allowed regions are `oregon`, `ohio`, `virginia`, `frankfurt` and `singapore`. Static sites are
served from the Render CDN and ignore the region.

1762.content:
| Capability           | Action                                      | Parameters                   |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `render-static-site` | `redeploy`, `rollback`, `suspend`, `resume` | as above, without `imageUrl` |

1764.content: `redeploy` and `rollback` return the Render deploy id as the action reference.

1765.content:
Health combines suspension, the latest deploy (live is healthy, failed is unhealthy, in progress is
degraded) and an HTTP probe of the public URL and health check path. Postgres and Key Value health
follow the status Render reports. Deploy history and logs are available for every resource; log
lines are redacted before they are returned.

1766.content:
The API receives `DATABASE_URL` (internal connection string), `DATABASE_HOST`, `DATABASE_PORT`,
`DATABASE_USERNAME`, `DATABASE_PASSWORD` and `DATABASE_DATABASE`. The site receives `API_URL`.

1767.content:
Container services deploy a prebuilt image. Building from source is offered only for static
sites, and static site environment variables are available at build time only.

1768.content: A service cannot change type in place (web to private or back). Delete it or rename the resource.

1769.content:
Render cannot move a resource to another region, shrink Postgres storage or change the Postgres
major version in place. The adapter logs a warning and leaves those settings as they are.

1770.content:
Postgres high availability needs a plan with at least 1 CPU (size `medium` or larger) and
version 13 or later. On smaller plans the database runs without a standby and a warning is
logged.

1771.content:
Autoscaling needs a Professional workspace or higher. When Render refuses it, the service runs
the fixed `replicas` count. Render services run at least one instance; use `suspend` to stop one.

1772.content: Key Value is a single node, so `replicas` is not supported, and external access stays closed.

1773.content:
Render has no resource tags, so template tags are not applied. Render has no deletion protection
either: production resources are protected only by OrkStage approvals.

1774.content: Custom domains removed from the template are not removed from Render.

1775.content:
The adapter does not wait for deploys or database creation to finish. Health reports them as
degraded until they are live.

1777.content: Run PostgreSQL as Supabase projects and keep files in Supabase Storage. Access token, organization, regions, how the password is derived, triggers and limits.

1788.content:
The Supabase adapter is covered by unit tests. It has not been verified against a live
organization yet.

1789.content:
The Supabase adapter talks to the Supabase Management API (`https://api.supabase.com/v1`) and to
each project's Storage API. There is no OpenTofu, no module and no state store: Supabase keeps the
state, and the adapter finds its resources again by name.

1790.content:
| Template resource     | Capability                    | What gets created                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `database.postgresql` | `supabase-postgres` (default) | One Supabase project per resource |

1791.content:
| Template resource | Capability                   | What gets created                                     |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `object-storage`  | `supabase-storage` (default) | A Storage bucket inside a `supabase-postgres` project |

1792.content:
OrkStage creates a project named after the resource in the target's organization and region, then
waits (bounded, cancellable) until it reports `ACTIVE_HEALTHY`. The template `size` becomes the
compute size (`micro`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `xlarge`). On a free plan organization the size
is left to Supabase (Nano).

1794.content:
OrkStage creates a bucket named after the resource inside the project of the `supabase-postgres`
resource it depends on. Without that dependency, the deployment fails with a validation error
asking for `dependsOn`. `publicAccess` sets the bucket's public flag and is converged on every
apply.

1796.content:
**The database password is never stored.** OrkStage derives it from its encryption key (an HMAC
of `supabase:db:<target id>:<project name>`). The adapter turns that into a 32 character
alphanumeric password, sends it once when it creates the project, and derives it again whenever
it is needed.

1797.content:
Outputs carry only `secret_ref`. When a resource on another provider needs the credentials,
OrkStage calls the Supabase adapter's `readSecret`:

1799.content:
`supabase://<ref>/storage` returns `url` (project API URL), `serviceRoleKey` and `anonKey`,
read from the Management API each time.

1800.content: Values never appear in outputs, logs or error messages. Errors from Supabase are redacted.

1801.content:
| `config` field   | Required | Meaning                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organizationId` | yes      | Organization slug: the id in the dashboard URL (`https://supabase.com/dashboard/org/<slug>`), or the `slug` field of `GET /v1/organizations` |

1802.content:
Create a personal access token in the Supabase dashboard under Account, Access Tokens
(`https://supabase.com/dashboard/account/tokens`). The token acts as its owner, so use an account
that is a member of the target organization. An OAuth access token works too. It needs the scopes
`organizations:read`, `projects:read`, `projects:write`, `secrets:read`, `database:read`,
`database:write` (restore points) and `analytics:read` (logs).

1803.content: The secret behind `credentialRef` is the bare token or a JSON object:

1804.content:
Validation lists the organizations the token can see, checks that the configured slug is one of
them (the identity shown is the organization name), reports the plan and checks the region.

1806.content:
| Capability          | Action    | Parameters | Effect               |
| ------------------- | --------- | ---------- | -------------------- |
| `supabase-postgres` | `restart` | none       | Restarts the project |

1807.content:
| Capability          | Action  | Parameters | Effect             |
| ------------------- | ------- | ---------- | ------------------ |
| `supabase-postgres` | `pause` | none       | Pauses the project |

1808.content:
| Capability          | Action    | Parameters | Effect                   |
| ------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------------------ |
| `supabase-postgres` | `restore` | none       | Resumes a paused project |

1809.content:
| Capability          | Action   | Parameters                               | Effect                  |
| ------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `supabase-postgres` | `backup` | `name` (optional, at most 20 characters) | Creates a restore point |

1810.content:
Health checks the project status first (`ACTIVE_HEALTHY` continues, `COMING_UP` and other
transitions are degraded, paused or failed projects are unhealthy), then the health of the
database, REST, auth and storage services (database) or of storage and the bucket itself
(storage). The database service is critical; other services down only degrade.

1811.content: Logs are the last hour of the unified logs stream (`postgres_logs` or `storage_logs`).

1812.content:
Deleting a database deletes the whole project, including its buckets. OrkStage destroy
protection is what guards production.

1813.content:
Deleting a bucket empties it first, unless it was created for a production environment
(`deletion_protected`). A protected bucket that still has objects is not deleted.

1814.content: One Supabase project per database. Supabase picks the Postgres major version.

1815.content:
Free plan: Nano compute whatever the template asks, at most two active projects, 500 MB database,
1 GB storage and 50 MB per file. Projects pause after a week without activity; run `restore`.

1816.content: Compute size applies at creation only. Resize in the dashboard, which restarts the database.

1817.content: No high availability through the API. Read replicas are a separate paid option outside this adapter.

1818.content:
The direct host is IPv6 only unless the project has the paid IPv4 address option. IPv4 clients such as serverless functions
should use `poolerUrl`.

1819.content:
Storage has no versioning, lifecycle rules or tiers. The Management API cannot create S3 access
keys, so none are returned; create them in the dashboard if a client needs the S3 protocol.
OrkStage shares the project service role key instead.

1820.content:
Restore points depend on the organization plan. The `backup` action fails cleanly where they are
not offered.

1821.content:
The catalog price is the list price of the compute size (Micro 10, Small 15, Medium 60, Large 110,
XL 210 USD a month, disk 0.125 USD per GB after 8 GB). The organization plan fee is separate.

1823.content: Deploy web frontends as Vercel projects built from Git. Access token, team id, regions, environment variables from dependencies, triggers and limits.

1832.content: The Vercel adapter is covered by unit tests. It has not been verified against a live team yet.

1833.content:
The Vercel adapter deploys `web.frontend` resources as Vercel projects connected to a Git
repository, through the Vercel REST API. There is no OpenTofu and no state store: the Vercel
project itself is the state.

1834.content:
A typical mix is a Next.js frontend on Vercel, PostgreSQL on Supabase and files on AWS S3. See
mixing providers.

1835.content:
| Template resource | Capability                 | What gets created                                                                   |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `web.frontend`    | `vercel-project` (default) | Vercel project with preview deployments, custom domains and the global edge network |

1836.content: Each deployment converges the project, keyed by the resource name (the Vercel project name):

1837.content:
Creates the project (framework, repository, build, install and output settings, root
directory, function region, preview deployments) or patches the settings that differ.

1838.content:
Writes environment variables for the production and preview environments. Template
`environment` values and dependency connection settings (`<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`
and so on) are stored as `encrypted`. Dependency credentials (`<ID>_PASSWORD`, `<ID>_URL` with
credentials and so on) are stored as `sensitive`, which Vercel never shows again. Managed
variables removed from the template are deleted; variables you add by hand are left alone.

1840.content:
Starts a production deployment of the template branch when anything changed or the project has
never been deployed. A repeat with nothing to change makes no writes.

1841.content:
Outputs: `kind`, `project_id`, `url` (first custom domain, else the `vercel.app` domain),
`dashboard_url`, `framework`, `branch`, `health_check_path`.

1842.content:
Health combines the latest production deployment (`READY` is healthy, building or queued is
degraded, `ERROR` is unhealthy) with an HTTP check of `url` plus `healthCheckPath`. Logs are the
build and runtime events of the latest production deployment, redacted.

1843.content:
| `config` field | Required | Meaning                                                                                                                        |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `teamId`       | no       | Team id (`team_...`, Team settings, General). Every API call carries `?teamId=` when set. Omit it to use the personal account. |

1844.content: Create an access token under Account settings, Tokens:

1845.content:
Scope: the team that will own the projects, or your personal account when the target has no
`teamId`. A token scoped to another team fails validation.

1846.content: Expiration: pick one that matches your rotation policy. Validation reports an expired token.

1847.content: The secret behind `credentialRef` is the bare token or a JSON object:

1848.content:
The token never leaves the control plane process. It is sent only as the `Authorization` header to
`api.vercel.com` and is scrubbed from every error message.

1849.content:
Validation checks the team id format, the region, the token and project access. The identity shown
is the team slug or the username.

1850.content: Vercel builds from Git, so it must be able to read the repository before the first deployment:

1851.content:
GitHub: install the Vercel GitHub app on the organization or
account that owns the repository and grant it access to that repository. For a team target,
connect the app from the Vercel team (Team settings, Git).

1869.content: Connect a Vultr account with an API key, prepare the Object Storage state bucket, and see how OrkStage runs containers, databases and load balancers on Vultr.

1881.content:
The Vultr adapter is covered by unit tests and its OpenTofu modules pass `tofu validate`. It has
not been verified against a live account yet.

1882.content:
OrkStage creates Vultr resources with OpenTofu (provider `vultr/vultr` `~> 2.30`, verified with
2.33.1) from the modules in `orkstage-modules/modules/vultr`. Each resource has its own state file
in an Object Storage bucket of your account. Vultr has no serverless containers, so a container
service runs as Docker on cloud compute instances.

1883.content:
| Template resource | Capability      | What gets created            |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `network`         | `vpc` (default) | One VPC, a /20 in 10.0.0.0/8 |

| --------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `compute.container-service` | `instance-docker` (default) | One cloud compute instance per replica running the image with Docker, and a firewall group |

1885.content:
| Template resource     | Capability                   | What gets created                                                 |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database.postgresql` | `managed-postgres` (default) | Managed PostgreSQL in the VPC. `secret_ref` is `vultr-db://<id>`. |

1886.content:
| Template resource | Capability                 | What gets created                                                         |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cache.redis`     | `managed-valkey` (default) | Managed Valkey, Redis compatible, TLS. `secret_ref` is `vultr-db://<id>`. |

1887.content:
| Template resource | Capability                 | What gets created                                                                        |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `object-storage`  | `object-storage` (default) | One Object Storage subscription and one bucket. `secret_ref` is `vultr-objstore://<id>`. |

1888.content:
| Template resource | Capability                | What gets created                                  |
| ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `ingress`         | `load-balancer` (default) | One Vultr load balancer in the VPC for one service |

1889.content:
Each replica is an Ubuntu 24.04 instance on the cheapest `vc2` plan that fits `cpu` and
`memoryMiB` (override with `overrides.vultr.plan`). Cloud init installs Docker and runs the
image with the service environment, `--memory` and `--cpus` limits, and the port published. A
firewall group opens the port to the VPC, and to everyone only when the service is public and no
load balancer routes to it. Changing the image, the environment or the plan replaces the
instances, new ones first.

1890.content:
Credentials of Vultr databases and object storage the service depends on are added to the
container environment as `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_USERNAME`, `<ID>_PASSWORD`, `<ID>_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`<ID>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. They travel in the instance user data, which every administrator of the
Vultr account can read, and they are kept in the OpenTofu state. Set
`overrides.vultr.injectCredentials: false` to turn this off; the service then receives
`<ID>_CREDENTIALS_REF` only.

1891.content:
Before each apply, the plan is looked up in `GET /v2/databases/plans`: the cheapest plan for the
engine and region with at least the memory of the size (`micro` 1 GB, `small` 2 GB, `medium` 4 GB,
`large` 8 GB, `xlarge` 16 GB) and the right node count. PostgreSQL high availability adds a
standby; cache replicas add standbys, up to 3 nodes. The chosen plan is kept while the size does
not change. Override with `overrides.vultr.plan`, `engineVersion` (Valkey defaults to `7`)
and `timeZone`. Without `publicAccess`, only the VPC range is trusted.

1892.content:
`readSecret` answers `vultr-db://<id>` and `vultr-objstore://<id>` from the Vultr API (the public
host when there is one), so a frontend on another provider can be wired to them.

1893.content:
A Vultr load balancer has no path routing and one health check for all attached instances, so an
ingress serves exactly one service: HTTP on port 80 to the service port over the VPC, with the
service `healthCheckPath`. Routes to more than one service, or a `pathPrefix` other than `/`, fail
validation; create one ingress per service. TLS needs a domain that already points at the load
balancer (`overrides.vultr.autoSslDomain`). Without it the load balancer serves HTTP only.

1894.content:
| `config` field | Required | Example               | Meaning                                          |
| -------------- | -------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `stateBucket`  | yes      | `orkstage-state-acme` | Bucket that holds OpenTofu state. It must exist. |

1895.content:
| `config` field  | Required | Example                 | Meaning                                                                              |
| --------------- | -------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `stateEndpoint` | yes      | `ewr1.vultrobjects.com` | Object Storage hostname of the subscription that owns the bucket, without `https://` |

1896.content:
The runner receives them as `VULTR_API_KEY`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` for
one command. Validation calls `GET /v2/account` and shows the account name as the identity.

1897.content:
Use the API key of a Vultr user with these permissions: Manage Servers, Manage Firewall, Manage
Load Balancers, Manage Object Storage and Manage Managed Databases. If the key has an access
control list of allowed IP addresses, add the addresses of the OrkStage worker and runner.

1898.content:
Create one Object Storage subscription for state and a versioned bucket in it. With the Vultr API
(the key is read from your shell, never pasted into files):

1900.content:
State locking with a lock file is off: conditional writes are not confirmed on Vultr Object
Storage, and OrkStage already runs one operation per resource at a time.

1901.content:
Regions are Vultr region ids such as `ewr`, `ord`, `sao`, `fra` or `ams`. Not every service is in
every region:

1905.content:
| Capability        | Action    | Parameters | Effect                                                                   |
| ----------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `instance-docker` | `restart` | none       | Reboots every instance of the service; Docker starts the container again |

1906.content: No autoscaling: the service runs `max(replicas, autoscaling.minReplicas)` instances.

1907.content: The image must be pullable without registry credentials.

1908.content: During a rollout, the load balancer receives the new instances only after the apply finishes.

1909.content:
No availability zones and no NAT gateway: `availabilityZones` and `natGateway` are ignored, and
instances keep a public address for egress (inbound closed by the firewall group).

1910.content:
Database storage is fixed by the plan (`storageGiB` is not applied). Backups are daily and
managed by Vultr.

1911.content:
Object Storage tiers are performance tiers: `tier`, `retentionDays` and `publicAccess` are not
applied, and each resource is a billed subscription.

1912.content: Vultr has no deletion protection. Production deletes rely on OrkStage approvals.

1913.content: There is no log API for instances, so the console shows no service logs.

1914.content: Vultr Kubernetes Engine is not supported.

1916.content: The OrkStage components (console, Control API, worker, Postgres, Redis), the path from template to cloud, the deployment workflow and provider adapters.

1923.content:
| Component   | Role                                                                                                         |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Console** | Next.js app. It calls the API through its own origin, so cookies stay first party and the API needs no CORS. |

1924.content:
| Component       | Role                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Control API** | Authentication, tenancy, authorization, templates, instances and integrations. It records intent and enqueues jobs. It never calls a cloud while handling a request. |

1925.content:
| Component  | Role                                                                                                                                |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Worker** | Runs deployments, the health monitor, drift scans, email and webhook delivery. It is the only process that changes cloud resources. |

1926.content:
| Component    | Role                                                                                   |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Postgres** | Desired and known state, deployments and their steps, and the audit log (append only). |

1927.content:
| Component | Role                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Redis** | BullMQ queues and the concurrency slots of each cloud target. |

1928.content:
| Component           | Role                                                                      |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **OpenTofu runner** | Each `tofu` command runs in a throwaway container that the worker starts. |

1929.content:
The domain packages (`domain`, `templates`, `provisioning`) import no cloud SDK and no framework.
Provider code lives only in the `cloud-*` packages.

1930.content:
None of these steps touches a cloud. A deployment stores the `ResolvedInfrastructure` snapshot, so
OrkStage applies exactly what you previewed.

1931.content:
OrkStage creates all steps when the deployment is requested, so the console shows the whole plan at
once. A job carries only the deployment id. The worker persists each phase and resource step before
and after it runs.

1932.content:
If a worker crashes, BullMQ delivers the job again (its stalled job handling) and the deployment
resumes. Finished phases are skipped, and converged resources (same idempotency key) are not
applied again.

1933.content:
A failed resource skips only the resources that depend on it. Only transient failures (rate limits,
network errors, timeouts) are retried, with exponential backoff. Destructive operations are never
retried.

1934.content:
An instance has at most one active deployment, enforced by an atomic compare and set on its status.
Each cloud target has a configurable slot limit (`maxConcurrentDeployments`, kept in Redis).

1935.content: A deployment that needs approval is parked. Approving it puts it back in the queue.

1936.content:
ADR 0003
explains why the workflow runs on BullMQ rather than Temporal.

1937.content:
`CloudProviderAdapter` is the only way the platform touches a cloud. It defines `validateTarget`,
`capabilities`, an idempotent `ensureResource`, `deleteResource`, `getResource` and `checkHealth`, plus
optional logs, metrics, plan and existence probes. One shared contract test suite runs against every
adapter.

1938.content:
| Adapter           | Status                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AWS (`cloud-aws`) | Real. Provisions with OpenTofu, checks health with the AWS SDK, reads CloudWatch logs and assumes a role in each connected account. |

1939.content:
| Adapter             | Status                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mock (`cloud-mock`) | Deterministic simulation of AWS, Azure or OCI, chosen per target, with injectable failures, latency, health overrides and drift. Everything it creates is labeled simulated. |

1940.content:
| Adapter                                                                                     | Status                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, DigitalOcean, Vultr, CoreWeave, Magalu Cloud (`cloud-<provider>`) | Preview. OpenTofu adapters covered by tests and `tofu validate`, not yet proven on live accounts. Off by default behind a feature flag per provider. See providers. |

1941.content:
| Adapter                  | Status                                                                |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Vercel, Render, Supabase | Preview. Adapters that call the platform APIs, behind the same flags. |

1942.content:
The database holds **desired** state (templates and instance configuration) and **known** state (what
OrkStage recorded). The providers hold **actual** state. Each resource row has a knowledge state and a
drift status. Health checks read actual state again on every tick, and the drift scan plans applied
resources again on real providers.

1943.content:
All tenants share one database, and every row a tenant owns carries an explicit `tenantId`. Isolation
has four layers, in order: the request principal, query scoping by membership, a CASL check on the
loaded record, and the audit log.

1944.content:
Sessions are opaque and stored on the server. Requests need a CSRF header, the API allows no CORS,
secrets are stored as references only, provider credentials never reach the browser and the audit log
is append only. See Security hardening and
ADR 0004.

1946.content: What to back up when you host OrkStage (Postgres, OpenTofu state, secrets), how to recover, and what OrkStage does for the backups of managed instances.

1950.content:
OrkStage does not ship a backup tool for its own control plane yet. You back up the stores it
depends on, and this page lists them.

1951.content:
| Store        | What it holds                                                                                                                          | How to protect it                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Postgres** | Tenants, users, templates, instances, known resource state, deployments, the audit log, webhook secrets (encrypted) and API key hashes | This is the one store you must back up. Use the automated backups and point in time recovery of your managed database, or run `pg_dump` on a schedule. |

1952.content:
| Store     | What it holds                                  | How to protect it                                                                                                                                 |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Redis** | Queues, concurrency slots and simulation state | You can lose it. Jobs carry only ids, and deployments resume from Postgres. Persistence (`appendonly yes` in the Compose file) shortens recovery. |

1953.content:
| Store              | What it holds                                                   | How to protect it                                                                             |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **OpenTofu state** | One state file per AWS resource, in S3 in each customer account | The state bucket must have versioning, so you can restore an earlier version of a state file. |

1954.content:
| Store       | What it holds                                                               | How to protect it                                                                                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Secrets** | `SESSION_SECRET`, `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the license key and OIDC client secrets | Keep them in your secret store. If you lose `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the stored webhook signing secrets become unreadable, and you must rotate them. |

1955.content: Test your restores. Until you have restored a backup, you do not know that it works.

1956.content: Restore Postgres to a new database and point `DATABASE_URL` at it.

1957.content:
Start the API and the worker with the same `ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `SESSION_SECRET`. If the session
secret changed, users must sign in again.

1958.content:
Deployments that were running resume from their persisted steps. OrkStage does not apply
converged resources again.

1959.content:
The health monitor and the drift scan read actual state from the providers again, so the known
state catches up with reality.

1960.content:
Templates declare database backups (`backup.enabled`, and `retentionDays` up to 35). The
`production-backups` policy fails any production database without them. On AWS, these settings
set the RDS automated backup retention.

1962.content:
The destroy workflow has a **backup** phase that checks the backup policy. It does **not** yet
verify that a backup exists and can be restored.

1963.content: A backups API (last successful backup, restore to a new instance) is on the roadmap.

1997.content:
The flow uses the authorization code grant with PKCE (S256) and verifies `state` and `nonce`. The ID
token's signature is checked against the keys the provider publishes (its JWKS), not only the TLS of
the exchange. Accounts are linked only through an email address the provider has verified.

1998.content:
Microsoft Entra ID is the reference provider. Google and GitLab work through configuration alone but
have had less testing.

1999.content:
GitHub has no OpenID Connect for people, so it has an OAuth 2 flow of its own with the same `state`
and PKCE checks. Create an OAuth app (GitHub, Settings, Developer settings, OAuth Apps) with the
callback `<WEB_PUBLIC_URL>/api/v1/auth/oidc/github/callback`, then:

2000.content:
OrkStage asks for `read:user` and `user:email`, reads the person's id and emails once, and discards
the access token. Only the **primary, verified** email can link to an account; the GitHub user id
is the stable link afterwards, so a later email change at GitHub does not move the account.

2001.content: The same rules apply to every provider:

2002.content:
A person who signed in with this provider before gets the same account (by the provider's id,
never by email).

2003.content: Otherwise, a verified email links to the existing account with that email.

2004.content: Otherwise, pending invitations for that email create the account with their memberships.

2005.content:
Otherwise, when exactly one tenant lists the email's domain in **Allowed email domains**, the
person joins it as a viewer.

2006.content: Otherwise, there is no account: unknown people never get one by default.

2007.content:
Disabled accounts cannot sign in. Each person can see where they are signed in and sign other
devices out under **Your sessions** in the account menu.

names, for example `ORK_AZURE_CREDENTIALS`.

2037.content:
Rate limit counters live in Redis, so they hold across every API instance. Signed in requests are
counted per session or API key. Sign in routes are counted per client address, which is only as
trustworthy as the proxy that records it: put a load balancer or reverse proxy that appends the
client address to `X-Forwarded-For` (an AWS ALB, nginx with `proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`) in front
of the console, and leave `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS` at `1`. The console's own proxy passes an incoming
`X-Forwarded-For` through unchanged, so without such a proxy a client can pick the address the API
sees for sign in limits. If the API is exposed directly, set `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=0`.

2051.content: Create the OrkStage deployment role with an external id, prepare the OpenTofu state bucket, then register and validate an AWS account as a cloud target.

2059.content: Edit a target or rotate its credentials

2062.content: What OrkStage creates in your account

2063.content:
OrkStage never stores AWS keys for your accounts. In each account, the worker assumes a **deployment
role** with **AssumeRole and an external id**. It receives short lived credentials that last one hour
(`AWS_ROLE_SESSION_MINUTES`), stay in memory and are never persisted or logged. Every OpenTofu run gets
credentials that outlive its time limit, so a long apply never runs out halfway.

2064.content:
The deployment role can create and delete infrastructure. Use a dedicated AWS account for each
environment.

2065.content:
The API and the worker call STS with **their own** AWS identity, found through the default credential
chain. One identity serves every account you connect. Pick one:

2066.content:
**EC2 instance profile** (recommended on AWS): attach a role to the instance that runs OrkStage.
Containers reach the instance metadata only with a hop limit of 2:
`aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-... --http-put-response-hop-limit 2 --http-tokens required`.

2067.content:
**IAM user keys** anywhere else: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_REGION` in
the environment of the API and the worker (the `.env` of the production Compose file).

2068.content:
**An AWS CLI profile** on the development stack: `AWS_PROFILE=<name> pnpm platform:aws-real` in the
development workspace mounts your `~/.aws` read only.

2069.content: The identity needs only `infra/aws/orkstage-control-plane-policy.json` from the platform repository:

2070.content:
Narrow `sts:AssumeRole` to the list of role ARNs when you know them, and drop the second statement
when you use `env://` references only. Its ARN is the `ControlPlanePrincipalArn` of every role stack
below. Without an identity, Validate says so instead of reaching AWS.

2071.content:
Launch the CloudFormation template `infra/aws/orkstage-deployment-role.yaml` from the platform
repository once in each account you connect.

2072.content:
| Parameter                  | Value                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ControlPlanePrincipalArn` | ARN of the identity the OrkStage worker runs as, for example `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orkstage-worker`. |

2073.content:
| Parameter    | Value                                                                                       |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ExternalId` | A random shared secret of at least 16 characters (`openssl rand -hex 24`). Marked `NoEcho`. |

2075.content:
| Parameter            | Value                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `MaxSessionDuration` | Defaults to `3600` seconds. Raise it with `AWS_ROLE_SESSION_MINUTES` when OpenTofu runs may take longer than 55 minutes. |

2076.content: The stack outputs **`RoleArn`** and **`AccountId`**. You paste both into the cloud target.

2077.content:
Use a **different external id in each account**. With many accounts in one AWS Organization, the
same template works as a CloudFormation StackSet, with the external id as a parameter override per
account.

2079.content: manage EC2 and VPC, ECS, RDS, ElastiCache, ELB, Auto Scaling, Route 53 and ACM resources;

2081.content: read and write the OpenTofu state bucket `orkstage-tfstate-<account>-*`;

2082.content: pass `ork-*` roles to ECS tasks and EC2 only;

2083.content:
call `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` **on itself**, so OrkStage can check permissions before it
deploys.

2084.content:
The template tracks the actions the OpenTofu modules need. A platform unit test fails when a module
needs an action that the policy does not grant.

2085.content:
Put the external id in a secret store that the control plane can read, and give OrkStage a reference
to it. Never paste the value itself.

2087.content:
OpenTofu state lives in S3, with one state file per resource (`orkstage/<physical-name>.tfstate`). In
a real account, the bucket must exist before the first deployment and must have:

2088.content:
the default name `orkstage-tfstate-<accountId>-<region>`, or the name you set in `stateBucket` on
the target;

2089.content: **versioning enabled**, so you can recover from a damaged state;

2092.content:
Locking uses the lock file that OpenTofu keeps in S3 (`use_lockfile`), so you do not need a DynamoDB
table.

2093.content:
Platform owners and admins can open **Cloud targets** in the console and click **Register cloud
target**. You can also call the API:

2094.content:
| `config` field | Meaning                                           |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `accountId`    | The 12 digit account id (the `AccountId` output). |

2097.content:
| `config` field | Meaning                                                                       |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dnsZone`      | Platform DNS zone for instance subdomains. It must already exist in Route 53. |

2098.content:
| `config` field | Meaning                                                                                                       |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ecsAmiId`     | Optional AMI for `ecs-ec2` capacity. When empty, OrkStage uses the latest ECS optimized AMI published in SSM. |

2099.content:
`config` must not contain secrets. The API rejects keys that look like secrets with
`422 SECRET_IN_CONFIG`, and a role from another account than `accountId` with `422 INVALID_CONFIG`. `credentialRef` must be an `env://` or `aws-sm://` reference, and any other
value is rejected. You can assign a target to one tenant (`tenantId`) or share it across tenants.

2101.content: resolves the external id and **assumes the role**;

2102.content: checks that the credentials belong to `accountId`;

2103.content: checks that the **state bucket** is reachable;

2104.content:
**simulates the role** against the actions each supported service needs, with
`iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`.

2105.content:
Missing actions for a service appear as **warnings** on the Validate button, because you may scope a
target to fewer services on purpose. If the role cannot call `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`, the
permission check is reported as skipped.

2106.content:
Click **Edit** on the target, or call `PATCH /api/v1/cloud/targets/:id`. You can change the name, the
role ARN, the credential reference, the DNS zone, the regions and the concurrency limit. The account
id and the state bucket are fixed, because existing resources and their state live there: a
different account is a new target. A region that still has resources, instances or profiles cannot
be removed. Any change other than the name or the concurrency limit clears the last validation, so
run **Validate** again.

2107.content: To rotate the external id without downtime:

2108.content: Update the role stack with the new `ExternalId`. From then on, only the new value works.

2109.content: Store the new value under a new secret name, for example `orkstage/aws/prod-external-id-2`.

2110.content: Edit the target and set the new reference, then **Validate**.

2111.content: Deployments that start after the edit use the new reference at once; the old secret can go.

2112.content:
Register one target per account and environment, each with its own role and external id, and create
one profile per environment that points at them (a tenant profile replaces the shared one for that
tenant when a customer has its own account). Targets in different accounts deploy at the same time
without sharing credentials: each OpenTofu container receives only its own target's.

2113.content:
The **Validate cloud targets** phase repeats these checks for each target and region the deployment
uses. This time it checks only the services being deployed, and it is strict. A missing permission
fails the phase with `AUTHORIZATION_ERROR` before any resource is touched, and the error names the
missing actions.

Every resource carries the platform's standard tags and a name of the form

2125.content: Profiles, services, volumes and networks of the OrkStage Compose stack, how the worker starts OpenTofu runners, and what to change before you share it.

2129.content: Before running it beyond your machine

2136.content:
`docker-compose.yml` in the `orkstage-dev` workspace
runs the whole platform from one shared image, built from the repositories checked out as
submodules. It is the way to evaluate OrkStage and to develop it. For a production host, use the
published images instead. Run the commands on this page from the
`orkstage-dev` checkout.

2137.content:
| Profile  | Adds                          | Shortcut                                            |
| -------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| *(none)* | Postgres 18, Redis 8, Mailpit | `pnpm local:up` (you then run the apps on the host) |

2138.content:
| Profile        | Adds                                  | Shortcut         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `aws-emulator` | MiniStack, a local AWS on port `4566` | `pnpm local:aws` |

2140.content:
| Profile         | Adds                                                                                       | Shortcut |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| `observability` | An OpenTelemetry collector that prints the telemetry it receives (ports `4317` and `4318`) |          |

2141.content:
| Service   | Image                     | Notes                                                                                                  |
| --------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `migrate` | `orkstage/platform:local` | Runs once: `prisma migrate deploy`, then the idempotent seed. The other platform services wait for it. |

2142.content:
| Service | Image                     | Notes                                                                                   |
| ------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `api`   | `orkstage/platform:local` | Port 4000. Its health check calls `/api/v1/readyz`, which tests the database and Redis. |

2143.content:
| Service  | Image                     | Notes                                                                           |
| -------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `worker` | `orkstage/platform:local` | Runs as root only so it can use the Docker socket to start OpenTofu containers. |

2145.content:
| Service       | Image                        | Notes                                                                 |
| ------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tofu-runner` | `orkstage/tofu-runner:local` | Built, never left running: OpenTofu 1.12.7 with the modules baked in. |

2146.content:
| Service                        | Image           | Notes                                               |
| ------------------------------ | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `postgres`, `redis`, `mailpit` | Upstream images | Data lives in the `pgdata` and `redisdata` volumes. |

2147.content:
| Service     | Image                                       | Notes                                                               |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ministack` | `ministackorg/ministack` (pinned by digest) | Needs the Docker socket. Its state lives in the `ministack` volume. |

2148.content:
One image (`infra/docker/platform.Dockerfile`) holds the API, the worker, the console and the
migration tooling. Each service starts it with a different command.

2149.content:
The worker reaches Docker through `/var/run/docker.sock` and starts `orkstage/tofu-runner:local`
containers on the Compose network. These variables wire it up:

2150.content:
| Variable     | Value in Compose             | Why                                     |
| ------------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `TOFU_IMAGE` | `orkstage/tofu-runner:local` | Runner image with the modules baked in. |

2151.content:
| Variable                | Value in Compose | Why                                                |
| ----------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `TOFU_MODULES_IN_IMAGE` | `true`           | Do not mount modules from the worker's filesystem. |

2152.content:
| Variable        | Value in Compose         | Why                                                    |
| --------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `TOFU_WORK_DIR` | `/var/lib/orkstage/tofu` | Location of the working directories inside the worker. |

2153.content:
| Variable           | Value in Compose     | Why                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `TOFU_WORK_VOLUME` | `orkstage-tofu-work` | The same directory as a named volume. The Docker daemon cannot see paths inside the worker container, so runners mount the volume instead. |

2154.content:
| Variable                   | Value in Compose        | Why                                          |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `TOFU_PLUGIN_CACHE_VOLUME` | `orkstage-tofu-plugins` | Provider plugin cache shared by all runners. |

2155.content:
| Variable              | Value in Compose   | Why                                   |
| --------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `TOFU_DOCKER_NETWORK` | `orkstage_default` | Lets runners reach MiniStack by name. |

2156.content:
Inside the network, MiniStack answers at `http://ministack:4566` (`AWS_EMULATOR_ENDPOINT`). Links in
the console still point to `http://localhost:4566`.

2157.content:
The Compose project is still named `orkstage`, the working name of the platform before the
OrkStage rebrand. Keeping it leaves existing volumes and the `orkstage_default` network
attached.

2158.content:
The Compose file is set up for local use. Before other people use the installation, change at least
the following.

2159.content:
Set `NODE_ENV=production` and `AUTH_DEV_LOGIN_ENABLED=false`, and configure an
OIDC provider. In production, the API and the
worker refuse to start while the dev login is enabled.

2160.content:
Generate `SESSION_SECRET` (at least 32 random characters) and `ENCRYPTION_KEY` (32 bytes, base64:
`openssl rand -base64 32`). Pass both from your secret store, not from the Compose file. In
production, startup fails without them.

2161.content:
Point `DATABASE_URL` and `REDIS_URL` at managed instances, or at instances you back up yourself, and
plan your backups.

2162.content:
Put the console and the API behind a proxy that terminates TLS. Set `WEB_PUBLIC_URL` and
`API_PUBLIC_URL` to their `https://` addresses. In production mode, cookies are marked `Secure`.

2163.content: Drop the `aws-emulator` profile and connect real AWS accounts.

2164.content:
The Docker socket gives the worker control of the host's Docker daemon. Run the worker on a dedicated
host. A runner based on ECS RunTask or Kubernetes Jobs is on the roadmap.

2165.content:
Published images (`ghcr.io/orkstage/platform`, `ghcr.io/orkstage/console`,
`ghcr.io/orkstage/tofu-runner`) are planned, and so is infrastructure code that runs the control plane
itself on AWS (ECS Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, ALB). Today you build the images from source.

2167.content: Follow an OrkStage installation through JSON logs with correlation ids, health endpoints, deployment events and the audit log. Metrics and tracing are planned.

2176.content:
The API and the worker write structured JSON logs (Pino) to stdout. Each line carries `service` and
`context` fields and the **correlation id** of the request. Tokens, secrets, cookies and
authorization headers are redacted. `LOG_LEVEL` sets the level (`info` by default).

2177.content:
The correlation id starts at the HTTP request (`x-correlation-id`) and travels into the deployment,
the OpenTofu runs, the audit events and the webhook deliveries. Search your log store for it to
follow one operation end to end.

2178.content:
| Endpoint              | Meaning                            |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/v1/healthz` | Liveness: the API process answers. |

2179.content:
| Endpoint             | Meaning                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/v1/readyz` | Readiness: Postgres and Redis are reachable. The Compose health check calls it. |

2180.content:
**Deployments**: every step with its duration, attempts and failure class, plus the event log and
the Gantt timeline.

2181.content: **Overview**: instances, deployments, failures and incidents, with trends.

2182.content: **Audit log**: every change, filtered by tenant (`GET /audit`).

2183.content: **Webhook deliveries**: status, attempts and the last error of each endpoint.

2184.content:
The API and the worker export OpenTelemetry traces and metrics over OTLP when
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set (for example `http://otel-collector:4318`). Without it, nothing
is loaded and nothing is exported. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and the other standard `OTEL_*`
variables work as usual, so a hosted backend (Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Datadog) can receive the
data directly.

2185.content:
Incoming HTTP requests (the health probes are left out), outgoing `fetch` calls (provider APIs,
webhooks), Redis and Prisma queries.

2186.content:
Queue jobs continue the trace of the request that queued them: a deployment shows as one trace
from `POST /instances/:id/deploy` through the worker's `job deployments` span.

Deploy an instance, then open Jaeger at http://localhost:16686 (service `orkstage-api`) for the trace,

2200.content: Targets for running OrkStage, not guarantees to customers. Each one names the metric that measures it.

2201.content:

| API availability | 99.9% of requests without a 5xx | `http.server.request.duration` by status |

| -------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Control plane read latency | p95 under 300 ms for `GET` | `http.server.request.duration` |

| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

Alert on a burn rate (for example 2% of the monthly error budget in one hour), not on single
failures. Until dashboards exist, also alert on `readyz`, container restarts and `deployment.failed`
webhooks.

2208.content: How OrkStage runs OpenTofu in throwaway containers, keeps one S3 state per resource without secrets, plans before apply and scans for drift.

2213.content: What is approved is what is applied

2218.content:
OrkStage provisions AWS with OpenTofu modules in `infra/tofu/modules/aws/*`, one module per logical
resource type.
ADR 0005 records the
design.

2219.content:
The worker never runs OpenTofu in its own process. Every `tofu` command runs in a **throwaway
container**: the pinned `ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.12.9` image, or the `tofu-runner` image with
the modules baked in.

2220.content:
The module library is mounted read only, or baked into the image. Providers come from a plugin
cache volume that all runners share.

2221.content:
Credentials reach **that one container only**, as environment variables. They never appear in
files, command lines or state.

2222.content: Each command has a hard timeout (`TOFU_TIMEOUT_MINUTES`, 45 by default) and can be cancelled.

2223.content:
Today the worker starts runners through the Docker socket, which gives it control of the host's
Docker daemon. A runner that uses ECS RunTask or a Kubernetes Job with a scoped role is on the
roadmap.

2224.content:
The state key is `orkstage/<physical-name>.tfstate`. There is one state for each resource, not one
for each instance or placement slot. This design:

2225.content: keeps the platform's own DAG, with progress, retries and failure isolation for each resource;

2226.content: limits the damage of a broken state file to one resource;

2227.content:
passes dependencies as module outputs that become inputs of the next module. Every module emits a
`kind` output, so the adapter wires them by type;

2228.content:
stores the exact root configuration next to the state (`.config.json`), so a destroy never depends
on a template that has changed since.

2229.content:
**Backend**: S3, with `use_lockfile` for locking, and encryption. On real AWS, you create the bucket
in advance with versioning and encryption, and OrkStage validates it before use (see
Connecting an AWS account). On an
emulator, OrkStage creates the bucket on first use.

2230.content:
An OpenTofu `ephemeral` resource generates each RDS master password, and the module writes it
through write only attributes (`password_wo`, `secret_string_wo`). Services receive the ARN of the
Secrets Manager secret as an ECS secret. We verified that the state holds `password: null`.

2231.content:
In the **Generate plan** phase, the worker runs a real `tofu plan` for every **existing** resource
whose desired state changed. It writes a summary for each resource to the deployment's event log:

2232.content:
A deletion or replacement makes the deployment **high risk**. A routine new revision of an ECS task
definition (for a new image digest) does not.

2233.content:
For a `production` instance, high risk **escalates** the deployment to `AWAITING_APPROVAL`, even
when the platform's own diff predicted only an update.

2234.content:
A resource the provider could not plan also escalates a `production` deployment to approval:
nobody approves changes nobody has seen.

2235.content: When no change is destructive, the approval step is marked skipped, with the reason.

2236.content: The deployment stores the provider plans (`plan.providerPlans`) for review.

2237.content:
Every OpenTofu command runs `tofu validate` after `init`, so a configuration error stops before any
plan or change.

2238.content:
The plan phase saves each provider plan to a file named after the deployment, in that resource's
working directory, next to a hash of the configuration it was made from. The apply phase then runs
`tofu apply <plan file>` instead of planning again:

2239.content:
If the configuration changed in between (for example a dependency was replaced earlier in the same
deployment), or the state changed (someone deployed or edited the resource), a **production** step
fails with a message that says so, and nothing is applied. Deploy again to plan and approve the
current changes. Other environments log a warning, plan again and apply.

2240.content:
The plan file holds attribute values, so it is used once and deleted, whether the apply worked or
not. Retries of a failed step plan again.

2241.content: Resources this deployment creates have no saved plan: the platform plan already lists them as new.

2242.content:
Previews and drift scans plan in working directories of their own, without the state lock, so they
never touch the directory of a running deployment.

2243.content:
Locking uses a lock file next to the state in the bucket (`use_lockfile`). A worker that is killed in
the middle of an apply can leave it behind; the next deployment of that resource then fails with
`Error acquiring the state lock` and prints the lock id. Before releasing it, make sure no
deployment of that instance is still running. Then, from the worker host:

2244.content:
The directory is the resource's working directory under `TOFU_WORK_DIR` (its name is printed in the
failing step's log), and the credentials are the target's (for AWS, a session of the deployment role).
Write down who released which lock and why in the instance's incident or change record: the release
itself happens outside OrkStage, so the audit log does not see it.

2245.content:
Every `DRIFT_CHECK_INTERVAL_MINUTES` (360 by default, `0` turns scans off), the worker plans each
applied resource on real providers again, from the snapshot it was deployed with. Any planned action
means someone changed the resource outside OrkStage. The resource then becomes `DRIFT_DETECTED`,
OrkStage writes an audit event and sends `instance.drift_detected`. The scan skips resources with
pending changes. A new deployment restores the configuration from the template.

2246.content:
When someone deletes a resource outside OrkStage, its recorded state outlives it. The AWS adapter
has a **live existence probe** for this case:

2247.content:
During **verification**, OrkStage probes any resource that is not healthy. If the resource no
longer exists, the step fails at once with
`Resource no longer exists at the provider. Redeploy to re-create it.` instead of waiting.

2248.content:
Verification waits in **one settle window of 5 minutes per deployment**, not one per resource, so a
slow service does not multiply the wait.

2249.content:
On the **next deployment**, the executor asks the provider whether converged resources still exist.
It recreates the missing ones instead of skipping them as unchanged.

2250.content:
The AWS adapter has been tested end to end against MiniStack with: VPC, subnets and security groups,
ECR, SQS with a dead letter queue, S3, Secrets Manager, RDS Postgres (real container), an ElastiCache
Valkey replication group (real container), an ALB with target groups and listener rules (live data
plane at `/_alb/<name>/`), an ECS Fargate service (real container, registered in the target group and
healthy), Route 53 and ACM. The adapter contract suite passes against it.

2279.content:
Every image is signed with cosign (keyless, from the release workflow) and carries an SBOM and
