| Command                                                                 | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ork upgrade [--instance SLUG] [--template-version V] [--yes] [--wait]` | Moves the instance to another published version of its template (default: the latest). Shows the plan first and asks for confirmation; resources the new version no longer has are deleted, and production changes that delete or replace resources wait for approval. |

| Command                                                 | What it does                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ork template publish [-f FILE] [--template-version V]` | Publishes a draft version so instances can use it. The server validates it again. Needs permission to publish templates. |

| Command                                                | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ork preview [--instance SLUG] [--template-version V]` | Shows the plan for the next deploy without applying it: the changes, their risk, the monthly cost and blocking issues. With `--template-version`, the plan of an upgrade or rollback to that published version. |

| Command                                               | What it does                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ork deploy [--instance SLUG] [--wait] [--timeout S]` | Deploys. With `--wait` it streams the deployment events and exits with a nonzero code if the deployment fails. `--timeout` defaults to 3600 seconds. |

| Command                                               | What it does                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ork destroy --instance SLUG --confirm SLUG [--wait]` | Destroys an instance. `--confirm` must repeat the slug. |

| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ork template validate [-f FILE] [--tenant SLUG]` | Calls `POST /templates/validate` and exits with 1 when the template is invalid. With `--tenant`, also checks that tenant's limits and feature flags. |

| Phase                                      | What happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Remove resources no longer in the template | Deletes resources the instance still has but the template no longer contains (after an upgrade, or a resource turned off by a variable), dependents first. The plan lists them as deletions, so production approval covers them. A destroy protected instance keeps them, with a warning. |

| Phase                                | What happens                                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Health and connectivity verification | Checks each resource until it is healthy, within one settle window. |

| Phase                             | What happens                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Configure secrets and connections | Wires connection references. Secret values stay in the secret store. |

| Phase                            | What happens                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Register observability, Finalize | Registers monitoring and moves the instance to `READY` or `DEGRADED`. |

| Phase                          | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Validate template and policies | The stored snapshot is checked again. A failing policy stops the deployment here. |

| Phase                  | What happens                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Validate cloud targets | Checks credentials, the state bucket and, on real AWS, the IAM permissions the deployed services need. |

| Phase               | What happens                                                                      |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Application rollout | Services run their images by digest, so the exact image never changes under them. |

| Phase         | What happens                                                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Generate plan | Builds the platform diff, plus a real `tofu plan` for each existing resource that changes. |

| Phase     | What happens                                                                      |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Resources | One step per resource, in dependency order. Independent branches run in parallel. |

| Phase    | What happens                                                                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Approval | Runs only for high risk production changes (see below). Otherwise it is skipped, with the reason. |

A **cloud target** is an account you register with a provider: an AWS account, an Azure
subscription or an OCI tenancy. It stores the allowed regions and configuration that is not secret.
Credentials are stored as references, never as values.

A **deployment** applies a plan in the background. The worker runs fixed phases: validate, targets,
plan, approval (when needed), resources, rollout, configure, verify, observability and finalize.
A **deployment** applies the plan in the background with OpenTofu, following the dependency graph.

A **profile** gives a name to a setup for one environment: the cloud target, and optionally the
region, to use for each provider. For example, "Production Europe" can name `aws-prod` in
`eu-west-1` and `azure-prod` in `westeurope`, and "Production Brazil" the same accounts in
`sa-east-1` and `brazilsouth`. Platform owners and admins create profiles in **Profiles**, shared
with every tenant or for one tenant, and mark one **default** per environment.

A **public page** shows the title and description you set, component names and states, incidents
and maintenance. It never shows resource ids, providers, regions or alert details. Incidents that
OrkStage opened on its own read as a plain impact, such as "Degraded performance on Acme
production", and their automatic updates as plain sentences. Incidents and updates written by
people appear as written. Resolved incidents stay listed for 14 days. The public address is
answered with its own rate limits, and an address that is not public looks exactly like one that
does not exist.

A **template** (`apiVersion: platform/v1`, `kind: EnvironmentTemplate`) describes business intent,
never provider resource blocks. Examples: "a container service with two replicas", "a Postgres
database spread across availability zones", "private connectivity from api to database".

A **template** describes what the environment needs, without naming a provider. You write it
once and deploy it many times.
a `dns` resource whose `customDomain` is `optional` or `required` (it is `disabled` by default);
A `fail` result blocks the deployment. Custom templates go through the same policies.
a `web.frontend` resource (Vercel, Render and the other frontend providers).
A backups API (last successful backup, restore to a new instance) is on the roadmap.

A browser cannot add a custom header to a request for another site without a CORS preflight, and the
API allows no CORS requests from other origins. Other sites therefore cannot forge requests.
a connectivity strategy for each link;
A custom domain attaches to a resource that can serve one:

a custom domain was verified or could not be verified, its certificate was issued, or it expires
in 30, 14, 7 or 1 days;

A deletion or replacement makes the deployment **high risk**. A routine new revision of an ECS task
definition (for a new image digest) does not.

A deployment of a `production` instance stops at `AWAITING_APPROVAL` when the change is high risk.
That happens in two cases:
a deployment started, succeeded or failed, or a production deployment waits for approval;
A deployment that needs approval is parked. Approving it puts it back in the queue.

A diff against the known resources gives the **deployment plan** (create, update, delete,
unchanged) and its risk. This step never touches a cloud. The deployment stores a snapshot of the
plan, so OrkStage applies exactly what you previewed. See
Reviewing plan & cost.

A failed resource skips only the resources that depend on it, and unrelated branches finish.
Partial failure is a normal outcome, shown per resource. In this example the database fails, so
the API that depends on it is skipped, while storage and the cache finish:

A failed resource skips only the resources that depend on it. Only transient failures (rate limits,
network errors, timeouts) are retried, with exponential backoff. Destructive operations are never
retried.

A full access token works. A custom scoped token needs create, read, update and delete on `vpc`,
`app` and `database`, plus `account:read` and `tag:create`. Validation probes the VPC, App
Platform and database scopes and fails when a scope needed by the resources about to be deployed
is missing.

A host name that points to it, with ports 80 and 443 open (Caddy gets the certificate from
Let's Encrypt).

A hostname belongs to one instance on the whole platform. Adding a hostname that another instance
already has fails with `DOMAIN_TAKEN`, without saying which tenant has it. Hostnames inside the
platform zone are refused. A claim that failed verification does not hold the hostname: someone
who owns it can add it to their own instance.

A job carries only the deployment id. Steps are database rows, created when the deployment is
requested and updated before and after each action. Resuming a deployment means running the same
job again, which skips the phases that already finished. Temporal is worth another look if long
flows that wait on people, or very large fan out, appear.
Read ADR 0003

A key reaches only the endpoints that declare a scope. Endpoints without a scope, such as API key
management, answer `403 API_KEY_NOT_ALLOWED` to a key.

A Linux host with Docker Engine and Compose v2, 2 vCPU and 4 GB of memory at least, used only by
OrkStage: the worker starts OpenTofu containers through the Docker socket, which gives it control
of the host's Docker.

A listing page shows the description, every resource with its estimated monthly cost, the
placement slots and the providers each one allows, its tags, its triggers and the full
template source.

A module change alters the plan of existing resources. The next deployment of each instance shows
the change as a provider plan, and
destructive changes in production wait for approval.

A name has 2 to 63 characters: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter.
Other names get `422 INVALID_NAME`.

A network binds implicitly only to resources in its own slot. A database placed on another cloud
therefore does not depend on the AWS VPC.

A new image or setting replaces the container instances. New instances start before the old
ones stop, and the plan treats this as a routine rollout.

A new instance starts as a `DRAFT`, and nothing is provisioned until you
deploy it. Open **Instances**, then **New instance**. Creating an
instance needs a platform owner or admin role, or the customer owner or admin role in the tenant.

A person who signed in with this provider before gets the same account (by the provider's id,
never by email).
A placement slot is a named group of resources that an instance binds to one cloud target and region.

A plain string is also accepted and is taken as `clientSecret`. The values reach OpenTofu only as
runner environment variables (`ARM_TENANT_ID`, `ARM_CLIENT_ID`, `ARM_CLIENT_SECRET`,
`ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`). Workload identity federation, with no stored secret, is planned.

A platform owner changes flags in the console under **Settings > Feature flags**, for the whole
platform or for one tenant, or through the API:
a policy report and an approximate cost.

A PostgreSQL instance without a network gets a public IP with no authorized networks, reachable
only through Cloud SQL connectors.

A profile fills every slot at once with the account
and region it names for each provider; you can still change each slot. Tenant members, who do not
see cloud targets, place the instance by choosing a profile.

A provider is enabled when all three `OIDC_<KEY>_*` variables are set and the issuer contains no
`<placeholder>`. The keys `ENTRA`, `GOOGLE` and `GITLAB` get display names. Any other key is shown as
written. Register this redirect URI at the provider:

A Render Postgres or Key Value in the same workspace and region is wired with its internal
connection string and internal host name. This applies to services only: static sites are built
outside the private network.
A report that is not a ScanReport version 1 gets `422 INVALID_REPORT`.

A request for another tenant's record gets **404**, not 403, so the response does not reveal that
the record exists. The console receives the rules from `GET /me` only to hide what you cannot do.
The API remains the authority.

A resource the provider could not plan also escalates a `production` deployment to approval:
nobody approves changes nobody has seen.

A run against a local platform (`pnpm platform:up` in `orkstage-dev`) with the seeded simulation
targets. Output is shortened.
A runner that does not need the Docker socket, and the remaining items of the public backlog.
A service cannot change type in place (web to private or back). Delete it or rename the resource.
A session lasts 12 hours. Signing out revokes it.

A template declares **placement slots** such as `primary`, `data` and `storage`, and lists the
providers each slot accepts. Every resource names a slot, and an instance binds each slot to a target
and a region. Bind all slots to one AWS account and the template runs on a single cloud. Bind `data`
to Azure and the same template becomes multicloud.

A template describes **intent**, never provider resource blocks. The schema on this page comes from
`packages/templates/src/schema.ts`, the source of truth for the API, the console builder and the
CLI.

A template names resource types such as `database.postgresql` or `web.frontend`, never a provider.
When you create an instance, each placement slot is bound to a **cloud target** (one account,
project, team or workspace of a provider) and a region. The provider adapter behind that target
turns each resource into real infrastructure.

A trigger is a named action on one deployed resource, with default parameters: redeploy a
frontend, restart a service, take a database restore point. The provider decides which actions
exist; the console and `GET /instances/{id}/triggers` list them with their parameters.

A trigger is unavailable while its resource is not deployed, or when the provider of that
resource does not offer the action (for example a template that asks for `backup` on a provider
without on demand backups). The console shows the reason.

A trigger starts work at the provider and records the result: the provider deployment or backup
it started, a link when there is one, and a message. It does not wait for a build to finish; the
instance health and the provider deployment history show how that ends.

A Vultr load balancer has no path routing and one health check for all attached instances, so an
ingress serves exactly one service: HTTP on port 80 to the service port over the VPC, with the

validation; create one ingress per service. TLS needs a domain that already points at the load
balancer (`overrides.vultr.autoSslDomain`). Without it the load balancer serves HTTP only.

An **instance** binds each placement slot of the template to a cloud target and a region.

An **instance**, also called a **stage**, is one isolated, logical environment for one tenant. It
holds the services, database, cache, queue, storage, ingress and DNS, for example *Acme Production*
or *Acme Staging*. Each instance has an environment kind (`production`, `staging`, `development` or
`sandbox`), a template version, variable values and one placement binding per slot.

An **organization** runs one OrkStage installation. It serves **tenants**, the customers or teams
that own instances. Every record that belongs to a tenant carries its tenant id. A user sees a
tenant only through a membership with one of the roles. A tenant can have
**limits**.

An API key acts **with a role**. A tenant key uses `CustomerAdmin`, `CustomerDeveloper` or
`CustomerViewer`. A key for the whole organization uses `PlatformAdmin` or `PlatformOperator`.
Scopes then narrow what the role allows, so a key can never do more than its role.

standby; cache replicas add standbys, up to 3 nodes. The chosen plan is kept while the size does
not change. Override with `overrides.vultr.plan`, `engineVersion` (Valkey defaults to `7`)
and `timeZone`. Without `publicAccess`, only the VPC range is trusted.

Each placement slot of a template can go to a different provider, so you can put every part of an
app where it costs least. This page follows the built in **Web app on managed platforms** template

Each provider adapter publishes a **capability catalog**. For each logical resource type, it lists
the concrete service that implements it, with its features, regional gaps and static list prices.
For example, `database.postgresql` maps to `rds-postgres` on AWS, `flexible-server` on Azure and
`oci-postgresql` on OCI. The resolver picks the default, or the `implementation` the template

The **Overview** tab of an instance draws its topology. Every resource is a node, grouped by
provider, target and region. Dependency edges connect the nodes, and connectivity links carry the
strategy label, for example `public-tls-allowlist` between AWS and Azure. Node colors follow
health, and simulated resources carry a *simulated* label.

The **Plan & cost** tab of an instance runs a preview (`POST /instances/:id/preview`). The preview
compiles the template with the instance's variables and placements, then compares the result with
what OrkStage already knows about the instance. It never touches a cloud and saves nothing.

The **plan** resolves every resource, evaluates policies, estimates the monthly cost and picks a
connectivity strategy for each link between clouds. No cloud is touched at this step.

The **provider plan** deletes or replaces something. This is a real `tofu plan`, run for each
changed resource during the plan phase. It can find a replacement even when the platform diff
shows only an update, for example when an attribute forces replacement. Routine ECS task
definition revisions do not count.

The **Validate cloud targets** phase repeats these checks for each target and region the deployment
uses. This time it checks only the services being deployed, and it is strict. A missing permission
fails the phase with `AUTHORIZATION_ERROR` before any resource is touched, and the error names the
missing actions.

Variable names come from the resource id: `database` becomes `DATABASE`, `files` becomes `FILES`

`<ID>_HOST`, `<ID>_PORT`, `<ID>_URL`, `<ID>_BUCKET`, `<ID>_ENDPOINT` and `<ID>_REGION`. Each
credential field becomes `<ID>_<FIELD>`, with camel case turned into upper snake case
(`poolerUrl` becomes `POOLER_URL`, `secretAccessKey` becomes `SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`). When a name
comes from both, the credential wins and the variable is stored as sensitive.

When an instance is created, every slot it leaves unbound is bound from the profile it names, or
from the default profile of its environment: the tenant's own default before a shared one, the
exact environment before `any`. Each slot gets the profile's target for the first provider in the
slot's list that the profile has, with the profile's region or else the target's default region.

slots out of `bindings`; with the CLI, set `[instance].profile` and leave slots out of
`[placements]`.

When that happens, OrkStage marks the resource `DRIFT_DETECTED` with the planned actions, writes an
audit event and notifies owners and admins (`instance.drift_detected`). Resources with a pending
change are skipped, because that change is a deployment, not drift. **Deploy** restores the
template's configuration.

When the plan contains no high risk change, the approval step is marked skipped with the reason
`Not needed: no high-risk or destructive changes planned.` Instances in other environments
(`staging`, `development`, `sandbox`) never wait for approval.
